headline: Claude agents lean the same way as humans, but only about a third as far
verdict: Agents ordered 10.63 units under O and 10.04 under C, a gap of 0.60 (humans: 1.98 in the original study, 1.15 pooled across the three replications). Every agent stayed inside or next to the profit-maximizing 10–11, so the gap comes from choosing 11 more often under O (61% of orders) than under C (9%). Human orders were far more scattered: the spread between agents is about 0.3, against about 1.7 for people. The p-value is tiny only because agents barely vary; treat the 50 agents as one model, not 50 independent minds.
m_agents: 50 Claude sub-agents (Sonnet), 25 in O and 25 in C, assigned at random. Each is briefed as a paid lab participant with a random student persona (age, gender, major, degree level) and receives the original game instructions word for word, plus the replication’s note that demand is the sum of three standard dice. Each agent plays its own conversation, so it remembers every earlier day.
m_engine: Agents place orders only through a command-line game. The engine validates the order (whole number, 3–18), rolls three fair dice after the order, applies the O or C payoff rule, records everything, and shows the next day’s prompt in the same wording as the Qualtrics study. After day 25 each agent answers a comprehension question and describes its strategy in one sentence.
m_limits: All agents are one model family, so they are not independent samples. They may reason silently about the optimum, which people with a die and poker chips may not. Personas are a simple stand-in for a varied subject pool. No payments are at stake for agents, and agents were told they are participants, not that the study is about payment framing.
